---
title: "Naming what a detector found"
description: "A detector's crops, a classifier on top of them, and the class that is a statement about the annotation rather than about the picture."
mirrors: classification
---

A detector answers *how many objects are there and where*. A classifier answers *what is
this one picture of*. Putting them in that order - find the objects, cut them out, hand the
pieces to something that knows more classes than the detector does - is the second thing
people ask for after boxes, and it is the one join this package deliberately leaves to you.

This article is that join, on [BCCD](https://github.com/Shenggan/BCCD_Dataset), the same 364
photographs of blood smears [the detection article](blood-cells.qmd) uses. The detector is
published, so nothing here has to find the cells again.

**It does not end where it was meant to.** The classifier learns the three cell types almost
perfectly and fails completely at the one job it was added for, and the measurement that says
why is the most useful thing on the page.

**Where the numbers come from.** Every figure below was produced by R's
`vignette("classification")`, which runs this same sequence through `rplatypus` on one
machine; by `maju116/rplatypus#117` that vignette is the source and this article is the copy,
so the two walk the same sections and reach them by different routes - a configuration here,
constructors there.

## Cutting the objects out, which is a decision about the data

`DetectionEngine.crops()` returns arrays, and a classification run reads a directory or a
CSV. The step in between - writing the crops out - is not in this package, and `crops()`'s
own docstring says why: *which crops are worth keeping is a decision about the data rather
than about either model.*

BCCD arrives in Pascal VOC's layout, one flat directory of images beside one flat directory
of XML, so a CSV per split is the only wrangling - the detection article has those dozen
lines. With them, the published detector loads rather than trains:

```python
import pyplatypus as pp

published = pp.from_dict(
    {
        "task": "object_detection",
        "data": {
            "train_path": "bccd-train.csv",
            "validation_path": "bccd-val.csv",
            "test_path": "bccd-test.csv",
            "classes": ["RBC", "WBC", "Platelets"],
            "mode": "config_file",
        },
        "models": [
            {
                "name": "cells",
                "architecture": "yolo3",
                "input_shape": [416, 416],
                "weights": "bccd-yolo3",
                "fit": False,
            }
        ],
    }
)
detector = pp.build_engine(published)
detector.fit()

records = detector.crops("cells", "test", size=(96, 96))
```

One record per image, with `key`, `crops`, `boxes`, `scores`, `labels`, `names` and
`dropped`. **`size` letterboxes rather than stretches**, so a tall box keeps its shape - and
it also throws away the one thing that separates these three classes most cleanly. The median
side of an annotated object on the test split is 41 pixels for a platelet, 103 for a red cell
and 182 for a white one, a factor of four; brought to 96 x 96 they are all the same size.

### A crop needs a label, and the label is a decision

Each crop is labelled by what it overlaps: the best unclaimed annotated object at an overlap
of at least 0.5 gives its class, and a crop that matches nothing gets a fourth class. Naming
that class rather than dropping those crops is the decision, and `ClassificationData` argues
for naming - there is no background entry, so a picture of nothing in particular is a class
somebody has to name. Dropping them would train a classifier that believes every crop it will
ever see is a cell.

Written out as one directory per class, following the dataset's own three-way split, that is:

| split | RBC | WBC | Platelets | nothing | crops | nothing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| train | 2367 | 214 | 209 | 129 | 2919 | 4.4% |
| validation | 787 | 87 | 76 | 380 | 1330 | 28.6% |
| test | 638 | 71 | 64 | 312 | 1085 | 28.8% |

**Read the last column before anything else.** On the images the detector trained on, 4.4% of
its crops match no annotated object; on the two splits it has never seen, 28.6% and 28.8%. A
detector's output on its own training images is not the output it will give you, and the
factor here is about six.

## What the detector already answers

Before training anything it is worth asking what a second model could add. Of the crops that
**do** match an annotated object, how often was the detector's own class right? 2790 of 2790
on the training split, 950 of 950 on validation, 772 of 773 on test.

**One wrong out of 1,723 on the two splits the detector never trained on.** A detector's class
head sees the object at the scale it occurs, with the whole photograph around it; a classifier
sees a 96 x 96 crop with the scale normalised away. So naming the three cell types again is
not work worth doing, and what is left is the other column: between a quarter and a third of
what the detector hands over matches no annotated object at all. **The question this page can
usefully ask is not *what is this crop* but *is this crop anything*.**

## The classifier, and the metric that is not accuracy

```yaml
task: classification
data:
  train_path: crops/train
  validation_path: crops/valid
  test_path: crops/test
  mode: nested_dirs
  classes: [RBC, WBC, Platelets, nothing]
models:
  - name: cells
    input_shape: [96, 96]
    blocks: 3
    filters: 16
    block_width: 2
    epochs: 60
    batch_size: 32
    optimizer: {name: adam, learning_rate: 0.001}
    augmentation:
      - {name: HorizontalFlip, params: {p: 0.5}}
      - {name: VerticalFlip, params: {p: 0.5}}
      - {name: RandomRotate90, params: {p: 0.5}}
    metrics: [{name: auc}, {name: balanced_accuracy}, {name: f1}]
    callbacks:
      - {name: cosine_annealing}
      - {name: early_stopping, monitor: val_auc, patience: 15, restore_best: true}
seed: 1
```

No `encoder`, so the contracting path is this package's own; `block_width` rather than another
level, because halving a 96-pixel crop four times leaves a platelet with nothing, and a crop
of one cell is the case that lever is for.

`ClassificationEngine.balance()` is worth reading before the fit rather than after it, because
the prevalence is what every later decision turns on: 81.1% RBC, 7.3% WBC, 7.2% Platelets,
4.4% nothing, and the engine's own remark under the table says that below about 10% a metric
read off the hard prediction stops telling a model from a collapse. That is why `auc` is the
default here and `accuracy` is offered rather than chosen.

Training AUC reaches 0.9972 against a validation AUC of 0.8829, and the loss is the clearer
half: the training loss falls to 0.047 while the validation loss **rises** from 1.53 to 1.87.
The model is memorising crops. Early stopping restored epoch 29 of 44 - the best `val_auc`,
which is what it was told to watch.

**The scoring table's `best_epoch` says 29 too, and this page is why it does.** That column
was the lowest validation *loss*, read off the history whatever the callback was watching, so
on a run like this one - loss rising from the first epoch while the AUC keeps improving - the
row named one epoch and scored another. Writing this page printed the two side by side, which
is how anybody noticed; `pyplatypus#398` fixed it in `0.8.0a68`.

## Scoring per class, because the mean is the commonest class

`evaluate("test")` reports AUC 0.8781, balanced accuracy 0.7210 and F1 0.6784, and an
accuracy of 0.729 - against **0.588 for a model that answers `RBC` to everything**. That pair
is the whole argument for the default metric: a reader told only the first would believe
something had been learned about all four classes.

The confusion says where it went, with the truth down the side:

| | RBC | WBC | Platelets | nothing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **RBC** | 638 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **WBC** | 0 | 71 | 0 | 0 |
| **Platelets** | 0 | 1 | 50 | 13 |
| **nothing** | 254 | 5 | 21 | 32 |

The three cell types are nearly perfect. The fourth class is a rout: 32 of 312, with 254 of
them called a red cell.

### Two things that do not help, measured rather than assumed

A second seed of the same recipe, and the loss that exists for exactly this problem - focal
cross-entropy, which loses interest in what it already gets right:

| arm | auc | balanced accuracy | share of alarms rejected |
|---|---|---|---|
| seed 1 | 0.8781 | 0.7210 | 0.103 |
| seed 2 | 0.8668 | 0.7152 | 0.125 |
| focal | 0.8783 | 0.7464 | 0.109 |

Two seeds of one recipe differ by 0.0112 of AUC and focal loss moves it by 0.0003, two orders
apart in this run and the same order in the one before it - and **two runs are not a spread**,
so neither figure is worth a conclusion on its own. The column that can carry one is the last:
the share of the detector's unmatched boxes that the model rejects runs from 0.10 to 0.13
across all three, which is to say that none of them does it.

## The class that is not a picture of anything

The obvious repair is not to make the classifier choose but to ask it for a probability -
`predict()` returns one row per image and one column per class - and reject a crop when
`nothing` is likely enough. The threshold is a decision about cost, so it is chosen on the
validation split and only then read on the test split. Precision before any of it is 0.7124,
the share of what the detector hands over that is an annotated object; the best any threshold
buys on the test split is 0.7409, at the cost of 4.9% of the real cells. **A gain of 0.028 of
precision for 38 cells, from a second model, a second dataset and a second training run.**

And a second model has to be worth more than the one number the first one already has.
Scoring the detector's own boxes at a range of `operating_point`s, with nothing trained:

| operating_point | boxes | cells kept | precision |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.50 | 1085 | 1.000 | 0.7124 |
| 0.70 | 1028 | 0.972 | 0.7305 |
| 0.80 | 990 | 0.955 | 0.7455 |
| 0.90 | 942 | 0.928 | 0.7611 |
| 0.95 | 907 | 0.899 | 0.7663 |
| 0.99 | 773 | 0.811 | 0.8111 |

The first row reproduces the 1,085 crops, which is the control that this is the same set of
predictions read a second way. At 0.8 the detector keeps 0.955 of the cells against the
classifier's 0.951, at a precision of 0.7455 against 0.7409. **A number that is already in
the specification is on the same curve as a second model**, and that is the comparison a page
like this owes before it recommends anything.

So the rejector does not work, and the interesting question is why not. It is not the
threshold and not the loss. It is the label. Of the 312 unmatched boxes on the test split, 92
overlap no annotated object whatsoever, 182 barely touch one, 31 are off their object and 7
are a second box on an object some higher-scoring box already took. And they are not guesses:
their median score is 0.9864, against 0.9999 for the boxes that do match.

Looking at them settles it. They are cells - red cells whole and overlapping, out-of-focus
smudges of exactly the kind the platelet class is made of, and patches of the purple a white
cell is stained with. **`nothing` is not a picture of anything; it is a statement about the
annotation**, and the question *is this cell written down in the XML* is not answerable from a
picture of the cell.

One photograph makes the point better than the table does: on `BloodImage_00327` the
annotation has 2 objects and the detector finds 16 above its operating point, and on
`BloodImage_00249` it is 3 against 16. The extra boxes are red cells. BCCD annotates a subset
of what is in some of its photographs, and a model trained on 205 images of it learned to find
cells rather than to find annotations - which is the right thing to have learned and the
reason a quarter of its output scores as wrong.

**What this costs beyond this page**: a precision measured against an incomplete annotation is
a lower bound rather than an estimate, so the per-class precision in
[the detection article](blood-cells.qmd) understates the detector by an unknown amount.

## What this does not do

**It does not show a classifier earning its place.** On this dataset the detector already
names its objects correctly 99.94% of the time, so the second model has nothing to add. Where
one does earn its place is where the classes are **finer than the detector's**: a detector
that finds cells and a classifier that names twenty kinds of them, trained on crops whose
labels come from somewhere other than the boxes. The surface is the same one; only the labels
would differ.

**It is not a measurement of the annotation.** That a detector finds cells no annotation
mentions says the annotation is incomplete on those images; how incomplete, on which images
and for which class is a question somebody would have to answer by looking, and nothing here
did.

**The crops lose the scale.** Every one is 96 x 96 whatever it was cut from, so the single
most separable property of these three classes is gone before the classifier sees anything.
`size=None` keeps each crop as cut, and then they cannot be stacked into one batch without a
decision of your own.

**It is one small collection.** 205 training photographs at one magnification, stained one
way, and the three classes it holds are easy to tell apart by eye. **It is not a diagnostic
tool**, and a result from it is not a laboratory result.

## Notes on the machine

A GTX 1070: the detector is loaded rather than trained, cutting and writing 5,334 crops takes
about a minute, and each of the three classifiers is about two minutes. `answers()` returns a
row per image with the label and the chosen class, `predict_labels()` the labels alone and
`predict()` the probability matrix the thresholds above are read from.
